entities.canonical_name: Issue #219 — Add ix mcp subcommand: expose ix as a local MCP server
entities.human_summary: Add ix mcp subcommand: expose ix as a local MCP server — open.
entities.deep_summary:
## Summary

Add an `ix mcp` subcommand that runs ix as a local Model Context Protocol (MCP) server. Exposes a curated set of read + write tools to MCP-aware AI clients (Claude Code, Cursor, OpenCode, etc.) so the model can invoke ix operations directly without going through shell subprocess invocations.

This is **orthogonal to and complementary with `--format llm` (#206)**, not a replacement. `--format llm` shrinks the output payload; MCP changes how the call is made and discovered. Tool handlers internally render with the same compact format defined in #206.

## Motivation

Today, AI agents invoke ix via shell:
- ix-claude-plugin hooks shell out to `ix text`, `ix overview`, etc. and inject results as `additionalContext`.
- Skills under `skills/` instruct the model to run `ix <cmd> --format json` in its reasoning, which Claude Code executes as a `Bash` tool call.

This is fine but has friction:
- **Model has to know about ix.** The CLAUDE.md routing table is ~3-4 KB of context loaded into every session teaching the model what commands exist.
- **Shell escaping is fragile.** See #196 — multi-line patterns and backslash escapes blew up because the hook concatenated shell strings. MCP passes args as structured JSON; this class of bug disappears.
- **Per-invocation overhead.** Each shell call spawns a Node process (~50-200 ms before any actual work). For fast commands (`ix locate`, `ix entity`) startup dominates. A long-lived MCP server amortizes this.
- **No tool discovery.** Adding a new command requires updating CLAUDE.md prose. With MCP, tool schemas are auto-discovered at session start.

MCP solves the *transport + discovery* problem. `--format llm` solves the *payload size* problem. Both stack: a session that uses both gets the byte savings of `--format llm` on tool responses plus the discovery and shell-escape wins of MCP.

## Where the code lives

`ix mcp` subcommand inside `ix-cli`. Considered alternatives:

| | Approach | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| ix-cli subcommand (this proposal) | New `ix mcp` in this repo | OK. Single source of truth, reuses existing handlers + renderers, no version skew, works for every MCP client |
| Plugin-side wrapper in ix-claude-plugin | Plugin ships an MCP server that shells out to `ix` per call | Rejected. Reimplements logic, doesn't help other AI tools, per-call subprocess cost |
| Standalone `ix-mcp` repo | New repo, depends on the @ix/client package | Rejected. Three-repo coordination burden, separate release cadence |

Files (new):
- `ix-cli/src/cli/commands/mcp.ts` — registers `ix mcp` subcommand
- `ix-cli/src/mcp/server.ts` — MCP server boilerplate (uses `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk`)
- `ix-cli/src/mcp/tools/index.ts` — tool registry
- `ix-cli/src/mcp/tools/<command>.ts` — one file per tool, exposes the tool's JSON schema and wraps the existing CLI handler
- `ix-cli/src/mcp/format.ts` — shared response formatter, delegates to the `--format llm` renderers
- `docs/mcp.md` — user-facing setup guide

## Transport

**stdio only in v1.** Client spawns `ix mcp` as a subprocess; JSON-RPC over stdin/stdout. SSE/HTTP transports add lifecycle and security surface we don't need. If a remote use case appears, that is a v3 addition with explicit auth design.

## Tool catalog (v1 — 28 tools)

Tools map roughly 1:1 to CLI commands the model already invokes per CLAUDE.md routing. Naming is flat (`search`, `locate`, etc.); MCP clients namespace by server name (e.g., `ix:search` in Claude Code).

### Read tools — navigate (10)
`search`, `locate`, `explain`, `read`, `entity`, `overview`, `inventory`, `rank`, `stats`, `text`

### Read tools — relationships (6)
`callers`, `callees`, `contains`, `imports`, `imported_by`, `depends`

### Read tools — structural analysis (3)
`smells`, `subsystems`, `impact`

### Read tools — history & decisions (4)
`history`, `decisions`, `conflicts`, `briefing`

### Write tools (5, Pro-gated)
`decide`, `bug_create`, `bug_update`, `goal_create`, `plan_create`

Write tools are annotated as destructive in their MCP descriptions so clients (Claude Code, Cursor) can apply per-call confirmation policies.

### Deliberately not in v1
- `map`, `ingest` — expensive (seconds to minutes); defer to v2 with explicit time-cost annotations
- `docker`, `instance`, `status`, `doctor`, `upgrade`, `view`, `reset`, `config`, `savings` — ops/admin, not model-invoked
- `query` — deprecated per CLAUDE.md
- `diff`, `patches` — niche; add when explicit demand appears
- Workflow-aggregated tools (`investigate`, `audit`, `discover`) — see v2 below

## User controls (toggling tools and the server)

Users should be able to constrain what the MCP server exposes without editing every plugin manifest that registers it. v1 ships four layers of control, each addressing a different threat model:

### 1. Server kill switch
- Env: `IX_MCP_ENABLED=false`
- Config: `mcp.enabled: false` in `~/.ix/config`
- When disabled, `ix mcp` exits immediately with a clear stderr message. The MCP client treats this as server-not-available and falls back to whatever the model would do without ix tools.
- Use case: user doesn't want MCP at all, even if a plugin registers it.

### 2. Read-only mode
- Flag: `ix mcp --read-only`
- Env: `IX_MCP_READ_ONLY=1`
- Disables all 5 write tools (`decide`, `bug_create`, `bug_update`, `goal_create`, `plan_create`). Server still advertises the 23 read tools.
- Use case: CI runs, sandboxed contexts, demos, untrusted-model paths, "I want navigation but no state mutations."

### 3. Per-tool allowlist / blocklist
- `ix mcp --enable-tools search,locate,overview` — explicit allowlist (most restrictive)
- `ix mcp --disable-tools decide,read` — blocklist (more common)
- Env equivalents: `IX_MCP_ENABLED_TOOLS`, `IX_MCP_DISABLED_TOOLS`
- Same values readable from `~/.ix/config` so users don't repeat them per session
- Allowlist wins if both are set (warn at startup).
- Use case: lock down to a known-good subset; reduce session-context cost from tool descriptions.

### 4. Per-call confirmation (client-side)
Write tools are annotated as `destructive` in MCP tool metadata. Compatible clients (Claude Code, Cursor) honor the annotation and prompt the user before each call. The server just emits the annotation; the actual prompt policy lives with the client.
- Use case: "I'm OK with this tool existing but want explicit consent each time."

### Defaults
All four default to permissive: server enabled, full toolset, no filter, destructive annotation present (so client-side confirmation kicks in for writes). Users opt into restriction.

## Tool response format

Each tool returns `--format llm`-style text by default, optionally JSON if the caller passes `format: "json"` in its args. Internally, tool handlers call the same renderers Ix#206 ships. The MCP layer adds no per-call rendering; it just selects which renderer to invoke.

This is why **Ix#206 (`--format llm`) must land first**. The MCP server's reason for existing token-wise is to deliver compact responses; if `--format llm` isn't ready, the MCP server has nothing to render with.

## Config and auth

Reuse the existing CLI mechanisms with no new surface:
- Env: `IX_ENDPOINT`, `IX_ORG_ID`, `IX_HOME`, `IX_DEBUG`
- Files: `~/.ix/config`, workspace `.ix/config`
- The MCP server is the same logical client as `ix` CLI; same `IxClient`, same `getEndpoint`.

The server probes backend health and schema version at startup (same as today's CLI commands).

## State and caching

V1: stateless. Each tool call hits the backend. No in-process cache.

V2 follow-up: TTL cache for read-heavy reads (`entity`, `overview`, `read`) that don't change mid-session. Per-tool TTLs.

## Build / install impact

- New dependency: `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` (~50 KB minified, no native bindings)
- Bundle size of `ix` increases marginally; no install-script changes
- `ix mcp` is discoverable via `ix --help` so users find it the same way they find other subcommands

## Test strategy

- **Unit:** per-tool handler tests with mocked `IxClient`, assert schema validation and response shape
- **Integration:** spin up `ix mcp` as a subprocess in a vitest test, drive it with the MCP client SDK, assert tool list + call responses against running memory-layer
- **Manual:** Claude Code and Cursor sessions with the server registered; verify auto-discovery, tool execution, error paths

## Adopter-side work

Tracked in ix-infrastructure/ix-claude-plugin#22 (analogous to plugin#21 for `--format llm`). Scope on the plugin side:
- `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` gets an `mcpServers.ix` entry pointing at `ix mcp`
- Skills under `skills/` migrate from `ix <cmd> --format json` invocations to `ix:<tool>` MCP tool calls where the call is model-invoked
- Hooks under `hooks/` stay on CLI; they fire on shell events, not model events, so MCP doesn't help them

Other adopters (ix-cursor-plugin, ix-codex-plugin, ix-opencode-plugin, ix-gemini-plugin) get analogous adoption issues filed in their respective repos.

## Decisions locked in

- **Subcommand name:** `ix mcp`
- **Transport:** stdio only in v1
- **Code home:** ix-cli subcommand (Option A from the alternatives table)
- **Tool naming:** flat names (`search`, `subsystems`, ...); MCP clients namespace by server
- **Response format:** delegates to `--format llm` renderers from Ix#206; not a separate format
- **Config:** reuses existing `IxClient`/env/config files, no new mechanism
- **State:** stateless v1; caching deferred to v2
- **User controls:** four-layer model (server kill switch, read-only mode, per-tool allow/blocklist, MCP-annotated destructive flag for client-side confirmation). All default to permissive.
- **Per-call confirmation:** server emits the `destructive` annotation on write tools; the actual per-call prompt policy lives with the MCP client.

## Out of scope for v1 (named explicitly so they don't sneak in)

- Workflow-aggregated tools (`investigate`, `audit`, etc.); design once we have v1 usage data
- Streaming responses
- Result caching
- `map`, `ingest`, or any expensive/destructive operation
- SSE / remote transport
- Server-side rate limiting or per-session metrics
- Auth beyond the existing IxClient mechanism

## Open questions

1. **Write tools in v1?** Currently planned to ship 5 write tools (`decide`, `bug_create`, etc.) annotated as destructive so clients can prompt; the new `--read-only` flag lets users disable them per-session. Alternative: defer all write tools to v2 and keep v1 purely read-only. Trade-off: read-only v1 ships sooner with smaller surface; write-included v1 means skills don't need to fall back to CLI for the write paths.
2. **Tool description length budget.** Every tool description is permanent session context. Cap at ~150 chars/tool? At 28 tools that is a 4 KB ceiling.
3. **Subcommand visibility:** should `ix mcp` show up in `ix --help`? Lean yes; discoverability beats hiding.

## Dependencies and sequencing

Hard prerequisite: **Ix#206 (`--format llm`) must land first**, at least Tier 1 renderers. MCP tool responses depend on having compact renderers to call into. Once `--format llm` PR 1 ships, MCP work can begin.

## v2 / v3 follow-ups (not this issue)

- v2: workflow-aggregated tools, result caching, streaming for large responses, `map`/`ingest` exposure
- v3: SSE/HTTP transport for remote scenarios, MCP "resources" exposure (graph nodes as resources), subscribe-style updates

entities.canonical_name: Issue #349 — [bug] Windows installer — path with spaces
entities.human_summary: [bug] Windows installer — path with spaces — open.
entities.deep_summary:
## Description

The Windows installer fails during CLI installation when the Windows user profile/TEMP path contains a space.

In my case, the user profile is `C:\Users\Win 10`. The CLI archive downloads and extracts successfully, but the installer then resolves part of the path as `C:\Users\WIN10\~1` and fails because that path does not exist.

Using a TEMP directory without spaces allows the installation to complete successfully.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Use a Windows account with a profile path containing a space, such as `C:\Users\Win 10`.
2. Run:

   ```powershell
   irm https://ix-infra.com/install.ps1 | iex
   ```
3. Wait for the CLI installation stage after the archive has been downloaded and extracted.

## Expected behavior

The installer should correctly handle Windows user profile and temporary paths containing spaces and complete the CLI installation.

## Actual behavior

The archive downloads and extracts successfully, but the installer fails while resolving the temporary path.

Changing `TEMP` and `TMP` to a path without spaces, such as `C:\Temp`, allows the installation to succeed.

## CLI output

```text
[ok] Downloaded to C:\Users\WIN10\~1\AppData\Local\Temp\ix-0.8.1-windows-amd64.zip
Extracting CLI...
[ok] Extraction complete

Ix installer failed.
Error:
An object at the specified path C:\Users\WIN10\~1 does not exist.
```

## Environment

* OS: Windows
* Node: v24.18.0
* Ix version: 0.8.1

Reopening: closed automatically by the #352 merge, but the fix is not yet confirmed to resolve this.

#352 **has** shipped and is worth trying — it routes the installer's two scratch files (the CLI zip and the compose pull log) out of `TEMP` and into `IX_HOME`, which comes from `USERPROFILE` in its long form. Since you confirmed that pointing `TEMP`/`TMP` at a path without a space lets the install finish, moving off `TEMP` should fix it. `install.ps1` is served from `main`, so it is live now — no release needed.

But the mechanism the PR described did not hold up, and nobody has reproduced this on a machine with the failing profile, so the issue should stay open until you can confirm. Specifically:

- PowerShell's FileSystem provider **does** resolve 8.3 short segments on both Windows PowerShell 5.1 and 7 — `Test-Path C:\PROGRA~1` returns `True`, and `Get-Item`, `Expand-Archive` and `Remove-Item` all work on a real `WIN10~1` path.
- Your transcript shows the installer reaching `[ok] Extraction complete`. The two provider calls on the zip (`Test-Path -LiteralPath`, `Get-Item -LiteralPath`) run *before* extraction, so they succeeded on that short path.
- `An object at the specified path ... does not exist.` could not be reproduced from any of ~30 path-taking cmdlets, including every one the installer calls on those paths — they report `Cannot find path` instead.

The most likely remaining explanation is that 8.3 alias *creation* is disabled on that volume while `TEMP` still holds a stale short path, so nothing resolves it. #352 fixes that reading too, which is why it shipped.

**If you are able to help confirm**, two things would settle it:

1. Re-run `irm https://ix-infra.com/install.ps1 | iex` on the affected account with `TEMP`/`TMP` back at their original values, and say whether it completes.
2. If it still fails, the full error would pin it:
   ```powershell
   $env:TEMP
   fsutil 8dot3name query C:
   Test-Path $env:TEMP
   $Error[0] | Format-List * -Force
   ```

One small thing worth checking either way: the output above quotes the path as `C:\Users\WIN10\~1`, with a backslash before `~1`. We assumed that is a copy/paste artifact and the real path is `C:\Users\WIN10~1` (the 8.3 alias of `C:\Users\Win 10`), since a literal `~1` directory would be unusual — but if your console really did print it with the backslash, that changes the diagnosis and is worth knowing.

Thanks for the detailed report — the `TEMP`-without-spaces datapoint is what made the fix actionable.

entities.canonical_name: Issue #374 — [bug] JS and TS calls disappear across 500-file parse batches
entities.human_summary: [bug] JS and TS calls disappear across 500-file parse batches — closed.
entities.deep_summary:
## Description

`ix map` resolves JavaScript and TypeScript calls differently depending on which 500-file parse batch contains the caller and callee. A caller parsed before its imported definition loses its `CALLS` edge, while an equivalent caller in the definition's batch resolves correctly.

This makes `ix callers`, `ix callees`, and `ix impact` undercount production usage and can produce a low-risk assessment for a widely used symbol.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Create a fresh TypeScript repository with 515 tracked files.
2. Put `src/a-consumer.ts` near the start of `git ls-files`:

```ts
import { crossBatchTarget } from "src/z-target";

export function runCrossBatchTarget(): number {
  return crossBatchTarget();
}
```

3. Add 510 filler TypeScript files so that `src/z-target.ts` is outside the first 500-file batch:

```ts
export function crossBatchTarget(): number {
  return 42;
}
```

4. Add `src/zz-consumer.ts` after the target with the same import and call pattern.
5. Configure `baseUrl` as `.`, then run:

```sh
ix map . --silent
ix impact crossBatchTarget --kind function --depth 2 --format json
ix callees runCrossBatchTarget --kind function --format json
```

## Expected behavior

Both `runCrossBatchTarget` and the same-batch consumer are callers of `crossBatchTarget`. The early consumer's `callees` result contains `crossBatchTarget`.

## Actual behavior

Only the consumer in the target's batch is reported. The earlier consumer has no resolved callee.

The path-only global index identifies `src/z-target.ts`, but JavaScript and TypeScript definitions are not included in `fileQKeys` or `fileHasSymbol`. `resolveEdges` therefore cannot verify the imported destination and drops the cross-batch `CALLS` edge.

## CLI output

```json
{
  "summary": {
    "callers": 1,
    "callees": 0
  },
  "callerList": [
    {
      "kind": "function",
      "name": "runSameBatchTarget"
    }
  ]
}
```

`ix callees runCrossBatchTarget` returns zero results.

## Environment

- OS: macOS 26.6.1
- Node: v26.7.0
- Ix version: 0.9.1

Thank you for the issue — and for fixing it in the same breath. The report is precise about the mechanism (definitions landing in a later streamed batch than the caller), which is what made #375 straightforward to review against.

Tracked by **#375**, which is open with review comments. It carries `Fixes #374`, so this will close automatically when that lands.

The change itself is correct — the index construction mirrors `resolveEdges`' in-batch path exactly, so cross-batch and in-batch resolution agree on `dstQualifiedKey`. My open question is cost, not correctness: the prescan parses synchronously on the main thread while the streaming loop uses a worker pool, so every unchanged JS/TS file is re-read and re-parsed on each incremental `ix map`. Details and measurements are on the PR.

entities.canonical_name: Issue #376 — ix upgrade compares two unrelated version series to decide if Compass is stale
entities.human_summary: ix upgrade compares two unrelated version series to decide if Compass is stale — closed.
entities.deep_summary:
The bundled Compass is stamped with the **Ix** version; `ix-compass-dist` releases use their **own** series. `isNewer` compares them directly, so the check is only accidentally correct.

Verified on the shipped v0.9.1 linux tarball:

```
compass/.version = 0.9.1          # the Ix version, not a compass version
```

and the latest `ix-compass-dist` release is **v0.3.0** (2026-08-09).

`upgrade.ts` does `isNewer(compassLatest, compassCurrent)` — `isNewer("0.3.0", "0.9.1")` → `false`, so nothing happens and `ix view` keeps the correct bundled build. That is the right outcome, but only because Ix's numbers currently happen to be larger.

**The moment `ix-compass-dist` tags anything above the running Ix version** — v1.0.0, or just v0.9.2 — `isNewer` returns true and `ix upgrade` replaces a correct, newer bundled Compass with the dist build. That is the same failure v0.9.1 just fixed (#365/#366), reached by a different route: there the stamp was missing so `current` read as `none`; here the stamp is present but denominated in the wrong series.

Options:
- Stamp the bundle with the **compass** version the release was built from (v0.3.0 was built from `system-compass@7f98724`), so both sides of the comparison are the same series.
- Or stamp the source commit and compare identity rather than order — the question is really "is the installed bundle the one this CLI shipped with", not "is it numerically older".

Either way, `getInstalledCompassVersion` and `writeCache(compassLatest)` should not be feeding two different numbering schemes into one `isNewer`.

entities.canonical_name: Issue #377 — [bug] Remapping keeps deleted and renamed symbols in the graph
entities.human_summary: [bug] Remapping keeps deleted and renamed symbols in the graph — closed.
entities.deep_summary:
## Description

After a successful incremental `ix map`, symbols removed by a rename or file deletion remain queryable in the graph. A deleted file can report a clean workspace even though its old nodes and incident edges are still present.

## Steps to reproduce
1. Create a small TypeScript project with `src/provider.ts` exporting `removedTarget` and `src/caller.ts` importing and calling it.
2. Run `ix map . --silent` and confirm `ix callers removedTarget --format json` returns the caller.
3. Either rename `removedTarget` in both files or delete `src/provider.ts`.
4. Run `ix map . --silent` again.
5. Run `ix locate removedTarget --format json`.

## Expected behavior

Entities no longer emitted by the current source should be removed with their incident edges. If a deleted provider file is later recreated, surviving callers should be re-ingested so their dependency edges are restored.

## Actual behavior

The old symbol remains resolvable after a rename, so repeated renames accumulate stale graph entities. Deleting the provider also leaves its old symbol and caller edge behind even though the map finishes successfully.

## CLI output

After deleting the provider and remapping with Ix 0.9.1:

```text
$ ix map . --silent
map: 3 files ...

$ ix locate removedTarget --format json
"resolvedTarget": { "kind": "function", "name": "removedTarget", "path": "src/provider.ts" }
```

## Environment
- OS: macOS 26.6.1
- Node: 26.7.0
- Ix version: 0.9.1

Thank you for the issue — this is a real gap, and one that quietly corrupts the graph rather than failing loudly, which makes it worth more than its size suggests.

Tracked by **#378**, which is open with review comments and currently conflicting with `main`. It carries `Fixes #377`, so this will close automatically when that lands.

The approach is right (compare the previous patch manifest, emit explicit deletions, track dependents so a recreated file heals its callers). The blocking item on the PR is that `reconcileRemovedEntities` runs before `stripMapModeOps`, which means `ix map` after `ix ingest` deletes chunk nodes it never recreates — reproduced on the branch. Detail on the PR.

entities.canonical_name: Issue #379 — [bug] --kind silently selects among duplicate same-kind symbols
entities.human_summary: [bug] --kind silently selects among duplicate same-kind symbols — closed.
entities.deep_summary:
## Description

Passing `--kind` can silently select the first result when multiple exact-name candidates have the same requested kind. Because resolution completes before ambiguity handling, an accompanying `--pick` is ignored as well.

## Steps to reproduce
1. Create two TypeScript files that each export a class named `DuplicateService`.
2. Give the first class one member and the second class two members so the selected target is observable.
3. Run `ix map . --silent`.
4. Run `ix impact DuplicateService --kind class --format json`.
5. Run `ix impact DuplicateService --kind class --pick 2 --format json`.

## Expected behavior

`--kind class` should filter out other kinds but remain ambiguous when multiple classes still match. Adding `--pick 2` should select the second class.

## Actual behavior

Both commands silently select the first class and report one member. The second command ignores `--pick 2`.

Without `--kind`, the same fixture correctly reports both candidates:

```text
Ambiguous symbol "DuplicateService":
  1. class ... DuplicateService in src/alpha/DuplicateService.ts
  2. class ... DuplicateService in src/beta/DuplicateService.ts
```

## CLI output

```json
{
  "resolvedTarget": {
    "kind": "class",
    "name": "DuplicateService"
  },
  "summary": {
    "members": 1
  }
}
```

entities.canonical_name: Issue #383 — [bug] Codex hooks and CLI subprocess calls fail on native Windows
entities.human_summary: [bug] Codex hooks and CLI subprocess calls fail on native Windows — open.
entities.deep_summary:
## Description

The official Ix Codex integration installs on native Windows, and the Ix CLI/backend work, but the installed Codex hooks cannot execute. This prevents automatic context injection and graph refresh unless users patch the installed integration locally.

There appear to be two independent Windows process-launching problems:

1. The generated Codex hook commands use `/bin/sh -lc ...`. Native Windows does not provide `/bin/sh`.
2. The installed Python integration invokes `ix` with calls such as `subprocess.run(["ix", ...])` / `Popen(["ix", ...])`. On Windows, the installed command is `ix.cmd`. Python's Windows `CreateProcess` cannot execute a `.cmd` file directly without a command shell, so these calls fail with `WinError 2`, even though `shutil.which("ix")` resolves `ix.CMD` and the same command works interactively in PowerShell.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Install Ix on Windows using the official PowerShell installer.
2. Install the official Codex integration/plugin.
3. Confirm that Ix itself works:

   ```powershell
   ix status --format json
   ```

4. Start Codex with hooks enabled and perform an action that should trigger an Ix hook.
5. Alternatively, run a minimal Python probe:

   ```python
   import shutil
   import subprocess

   print(shutil.which("ix"))  # resolves ...\ix.CMD
   subprocess.run(["ix", "status", "--format", "json"], check=True)
   ```

## Expected behavior

The official Codex integration should work on native Windows without modifying installed Ix/plugin files:

- hook commands should use a platform-compatible launcher;
- Python subprocess calls should launch the Windows CLI correctly;
- automatic Ix context injection and graph refresh should operate after installation.

## Actual behavior

- hook commands referencing `/bin/sh` cannot start on native Windows;
- direct Python subprocess calls to `ix` fail with `FileNotFoundError: [WinError 2]`;
- the CLI itself works normally when invoked from PowerShell as `ix`.

## Environment

- OS: Windows 11 Home, 10.0.26200
- PowerShell: 7.6.3
- Node.js: 22.23.0
- Python: 3.14.4
- Codex CLI: 0.147.0
- Ix: 0.9.1
- Ix Codex plugin: 2.4.0

## Request

Please make the generated Codex integration platform-aware so native Windows users can use the official hooks without local patches. Keeping generated/installed plugin files unmodified is important because local edits are overwritten or may conflict with future Ix updates.

Both causes are now covered, in the plugin repo — mirrored there as ix-codex-plugin#22, because GitHub closing keywords do not work across repositories and this issue would otherwise never auto-close.

| cause | fix |
|---|---|
| `/bin/sh -lc` in all five `hooks.json` commands | ix-codex-plugin#20 |
| `subprocess` not consulting `PATHEXT` for `ix.CMD` | ix-codex-plugin#19 |

Worth being explicit that **neither alone is enough**: #19's fix lives inside `common.py`, and until #20 lands the hook process never starts, so that code never runs. #19's own description scopes it to "the half that breaks the CLI" — it is the half that is unreachable without the other.

Leaving this open. Neither PR has been run on real Windows; both were written and tested on Linux, where the changed paths are no-ops or unit-tested in isolation. @tept-creator — a confirmation from a real Windows box after both merge is what should close this.

entities.canonical_name: Issue #385 — [bug] ix upgrade breaks Windows CLI when upgrading from 0.8.1 to 0.9.1
entities.human_summary: [bug] ix upgrade breaks Windows CLI when upgrading from 0.8.1 to 0.9.1 — open.
entities.deep_summary:
## Description

Running `ix upgrade` on Windows broke the installed Ix CLI while upgrading from version `0.8.1` to `0.9.1`.

Before the upgrade, `ix` worked normally. After the upgrade completed, invoking `ix` failed because the generated wrapper at `~\.ix\bin\ix.cmd` pointed to a CLI path that no longer existed.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Start with a working Ix `0.8.1` installation on Windows.
2. Run:

   ```powershell
   ix upgrade
   ```
3. After upgrading to `0.9.1`, run:

   ```powershell
   ix
   ```

## Expected behavior

`ix upgrade` should upgrade the CLI in place and leave the `ix` command functional.

After upgrading, `ix --version` should report `0.9.1` and all existing commands should continue to work.

## Actual behavior

After upgrading from `0.8.1` to `0.9.1`, the `ix` command became unusable.

The wrapper under:

```text
C:\Users\Win 10\.ix\bin\ix.cmd
```

attempted to execute:

```text
C:\Users\Win 10\.ix\bin\..\cli\ix.cmd
```

but that target was no longer available after the upgrade.

Re-running the full Windows installer restored the CLI.

## CLI output

```text
PS C:\Users\Win 10\Documents\project\coin> ix

'"C:\Users\Win 10\.ix\bin\..\cli\ix.cmd"' is not recognized as an internal or external command,
operable program or batch file.
```

## Environment

* OS: Windows
* Node: v24.18.0
* Ix version before upgrade: 0.8.1
* Ix version being upgraded to: 0.9.1

Thank you for the issue — this is an unusually good report. Naming the exact path the wrapper tried to execute is what made it diagnosable in one pass, and noting that reinstalling restored it confirmed the cause before anyone had to reproduce it.

## Unblocking you now

```powershell
irm https://ix-infra.com/install.ps1 | iex
```

That rewrites the launcher and restores the CLI, which matches what you already found. You should not need to uninstall first, and your graph and config are untouched — the breakage is only in `~\.ix\bin\ix.cmd`.

## What happened

You were on the wrong side of a one-way door.

`ix upgrade` before 0.9.0 refreshed only the **bash** shim (the one Git Bash uses) and never touched `~\.ix\bin\ix.cmd`, which is the launcher native PowerShell actually runs. Meanwhile the upgrade extracted the new CLI into a **version-nested** directory, so `~\.ix\cli\ix.cmd` — the path your launcher points at — stopped existing. Your wrapper was left aimed at a file the upgrade had just moved.

The layout half of this was fixed in #346 and shipped in v0.9.0. The catch is that `ix upgrade` is run by the version you are upgrading *from*, so 0.8.1 executed 0.8.1's code and the fix could not participate. **Anyone going from ≤0.8.1 to 0.9.x on Windows hits this**, and no change we ship can prevent it retroactively — which is precisely why it deserved its own fix rather than a "already fixed, please upgrade" reply.

Once you are on 0.9.1, future upgrades go through `refreshLaunchers()`, which rewrites the launcher for either layout. This is a one-time cost.

## What is changing

#386 makes the launcher diagnose itself. It checks its target before invoking it and, when it is missing, prints the cause and the reinstall command instead of cmd.exe's message naming the wrapper. That has to live in the batch file: at that point `ix doctor` is exactly as unreachable as `ix`, so nothing inside the CLI can reach you.

Your report also turned up a second bug in the same three lines: the old launcher never propagated the exit code, so **every** non-zero `ix` exit was reported to callers as success. That has been fixed alongside it.

I am leaving this issue open until someone confirms the new launcher on real Windows — I do not have a machine to run cmd.exe on, and I would rather not close it on tests alone.

One question, if you have a moment: does `ix --version` report `0.9.1` after reinstalling? That tells us whether the upgrade had already staged the new CLI correctly and only the launcher was wrong, or whether the payload needed replacing too.

Status check, since three separate changes touch this and it is not obvious from the outside which of them closes it.

**The forward path is complete.** Traced end to end on `main`:

- the release archive carries `ix.cmd` at its top level (`release.yml:309`), so the file the shim targets is genuinely in the tarball;
- `install.ps1` collapses that top level into a flat `$IX_HOME\cli\`, which is why `%~dp0..\cli\ix.cmd` resolves (#346, v0.9.0);
- `ix upgrade` re-derives the same layout — `soleChildDir(installDir) ?? installDir` (`upgrade.ts:1026`) — and `refreshLaunchers()` rewrites `bin\ix.cmd` to match, flat or nested, on every upgrade.

So an upgrade **from v0.9.0 or later** rewrites the shim to a target that exists.

**What cannot be fixed forward** is the population this was reported from: `ix upgrade` is executed by the version being upgraded *from*, so nothing shipped today reaches a v0.8.1 install. #386 is the recovery for exactly that — the launcher now checks its target before invoking it and prints the reinstall command, because once broken, `ix doctor` is as unreachable as `ix`.

**What is still missing is a Windows run.** Every piece above is asserted by tests and has never been executed by `cmd.exe` — #386 shipped as `Refs`, not `Fixes`, for that reason. This wants:

1. a v0.9.1 → v0.9.2 upgrade, confirming `ix --version` still works afterwards, and
2. a deliberately broken `bin\ix.cmd` (point it at a nonexistent target), confirming the recovery message prints rather than the raw `is not recognized` error.

That is what should close this, not another patch. Same standing requirement as #349 and #383.

entities.canonical_name: PR #365 — fix(release): stamp the bundled compass with the release it ships in
entities.human_summary: fix(release): stamp the bundled compass with the release it ships in — RESOLVED.
entities.deep_summary:
**This is the bug that made v0.9.0 revert its own compass.** Found while diagnosing an unrelated Windows tar failure on the GA upgrade path.

## What happens

The compass in the release tarball has no `.version` marker. So after `ix upgrade` replaces `$IX_HOME/cli/` — compass included — `getInstalledCompassVersion()` finds `index.html` but no stamp and returns `0.0.0`:

```
Compass update available: none → 0.2.0
```

`none` is a compass that was just shipped. `isNewer("0.2.0", "0.0.0")` is true, so the upgrader replaces it with `ix-compass-dist` v0.2.0 — published **2026-06-08**, two months before the fixes v0.9.0 exists to deliver. I checked that bundle: `smaller regions`, `__ix_tail__` all absent.

On Windows a separate tar failure (fixed in #366) masked it. Everywhere else the swap succeeds and the map silently reverts.

`install.sh` already writes this file after extracting, so a **fresh install was fine** — only the upgrade path lost the stamp, because the tarball it unpacks never had one.

## The fix

Stamp `compass/.version` at package time so the bundle declares its own provenance instead of relying on whoever unpacks it to guess.

The **Ix** version rather than a compass version: the bundle is built from compass `main` at release time, so it's always at least as new as any `ix-compass-dist` release cut before it. That makes the Ix version a monotonic stand-in, and a genuine dist release published later at a higher number is still offered normally. `install.sh` writes the dist number into the same file; either value suppresses the spurious update, and the stamp being present at all is what matters.

The repair path is untouched: a missing or broken bundle still has no `index.html`, still reads `0.0.0`, and still re-downloads.

## Both archives verify the stamp

`tar` and `7z` are trusted to carry a dot-named file, so both branches now check it's actually inside the artifact. Losing it produces **no error at all** — every upgrade just quietly reverts the compass — so it has to fail at packaging or not at all.

Simulated both paths locally: the stamp round-trips through `tar -czf` → `--strip-components=1` and reads back as the version, and the guard fires when the stamp is stripped from the archive.

## Note

v0.9.0 is already out with this defect. I cut [`ix-compass-dist` v0.3.0](https://github.com/ix-infrastructure/ix-compass-dist/releases/tag/v0.3.0) from compass `main` as the immediate mitigation — installed CLIs now pull the correct bundle, and anyone already reverted is repaired by upgrading again. This PR stops it recurring.

entities.canonical_name: PR #366 — fix(upgrade): pair the tar binary with the path form it understands
entities.human_summary: fix(upgrade): pair the tar binary with the path form it understands — RESOLVED.
entities.deep_summary:
The failure seen on the v0.9.0 upgrade path on Windows:

```
[!!] Compass extract failed: Command failed: tar -xzf /cygdrive/c/Users/ianja/AppData/Local/Temp/ix-compass-XOEabx/compass-0.2.0.tar.gz -C /cygdrive/c/Users/ianja/.ix/.compass-staging-55528 --strip-components=1
tar: Error opening archive: Failed to open '/cygdrive/c/Users/ianja/AppData/Local/Temp/ix-compass-XOEabx/compass-0.2.0.tar.gz'
```

## Cause

`installCompassBundle` rewrote its paths to Cygwin form whenever `cygpath` was on the box, then ran whatever `tar` PATH resolved to:

```js
if (process.platform === "win32") {
  try {
    tarFile = execFileSync("cygpath", ["-u", tarPath], …).trim();   // → /cygdrive/c/...
    tarDest = execFileSync("cygpath", ["-u", stagingDir], …).trim();
  } catch { /* use as-is */ }
}
execFileSync("tar", ["-xzf", tarFile, "-C", tarDest, …]);           // ← may be bsdtar
```

Two independent decisions, and the code assumed they agreed: *cygpath exists* ⟹ *tar is a Cygwin tar*.

Git for Windows supplies `cygpath`. Windows 10 1803+ supplies `System32\tar.exe`. On a machine with both — which is an ordinary Windows dev box — the rewrite happens and bsdtar, which has never heard of `/cygdrive/c`, is handed the result. The CLI extract sidesteps all of this by using `extractZipOnWindows`; this was the only remaining `tar` shell-out.

## Fix

Choose the binary and the path form as matched pairs, best first:

1. **System tar with native paths** — `System32\tar.exe` is unambiguous and isn't reached through any MSYS argument rewriting.
2. **PATH tar with native paths.**
3. **PATH tar with converted paths** — a genuine MSYS-only environment.

Trying rather than detecting, because "which tar is this" has no reliable answer and being wrong costs one failed extract into a scratch directory — which is now wiped between attempts, so the `index.html` check can't end up answering about the wreckage of an earlier try.

## Tests

The converter is injectable, because off Windows `cygpath` doesn't exist and every attempt would collapse to the native form — hiding the very inversion the test exists to catch. With a stub converter the ordering is provable anywhere.

Verified it fails against the old logic:

```
AssertionError: expected '/cygdrive/c/Temp/c.tar.gz' to be 'C:\Temp\c.tar.gz'
```

Seven new cases covering ordering, the no-cygpath path, never pairing a converted path with the system tar, and `systemTarPath` resolution via `SystemRoot`/`windir`. Full suite green — 648 tests, `tsc` and `eslint` clean.

## Related

This failure was masking a worse one: the bundled compass ships unversioned, so `ix upgrade` replaces it with an older `ix-compass-dist` build. #365 fixes that; here the extract merely failed, which is why Windows kept the correct compass and other platforms didn't.

entities.deep_summary:
## What

`explain`, `read`, `status`, `doctor` and `savings` advertised `text|json|llm` and rendered `text` when given `llm`. `docs/llm-format.md` documented that fallback as intentional — commands whose output is prose or verbatim source route to "the most compact existing form".

That holds for the *payload* and not for what surrounds it. `explain`'s prose is a rendering of `facts` + `role` + `importance`, so an agent can have the inputs and skip the paragraph. `read`'s source was arriving under a 4-column line-number gutter and two ANSI escapes per line. And `explain` is the first call most plugins make on any question, so the fallback was costing the most tokens on the hottest path.

## Measured

Against `--format json`, which the help text sent agents to as the workaround:

| command | json | llm | saved |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| explain | 1849 | 829 | **55%** |
| doctor | 682 | 470 | 31% |
| savings --detail | 1010 | 693 | 31% |
| read (40 lines) | 1661 | 1585 | 5% |
| status | 184 | 186 | −1% |

`read` gains 23% against `text` instead — 601 of those bytes are gutter and ANSI on a 40-line read.

**`status` is a wash on size and is in anyway**, for the explicit `stale=true|false` field: that is the question the command gets called to answer, and `text` only implied it through a warning line. Its unreachable-backend path now emits the spec's `error code=...` record so a consumer parses the failure the same way it parses a result.

## Notes

- **`read`'s content block is the one place the one-record-per-line invariant is relaxed.** The preceding `content lines=<n>` record makes the block self-delimiting, so a line of source can never be mistaken for a record.
- Still on text, now documented rather than silent: `diff --content` (verbatim hunks) and `ingest` (hidden implementation-detail command).
- Found while writing this: the `doctor` status ternary. A warning there is `{ok: false, warn: true}`, so checking `warn` on the `ok` branch reports every warning as a hard failure — the opposite of what `hasFailure` concludes two lines down. Caught by the test, fixed before it shipped.

## CLAUDE.md

The paragraph on this was wrong in both directions: it claimed the deprecated `query` advertises `llm` (it offers only `text|json`) and missed `doctor`, `savings` and `ingest`. It also never mentioned that `config`, `init`, `reset`, `upgrade`, `view`, `watch` and `docker` take no `--format` at all — `--format llm` there is an `unknown option` error, not a fallback, which is the one case where an agent following the doc's "pass it unconditionally" advice breaks.

That paragraph sits between the `IX-MEMORY` markers, which say not to hand-edit. **There is no generator for it in this repo** (only `scripts/disconnect.sh` touches the markers, and only to strip them), so I corrected it in place — but whatever regenerates it needs the same fix or this reverts on the next run.

## Test

51 files / 661 tests green, plus 13 new in `llm-tier5.test.ts` covering the records, zero-count survival, quoting of a multi-line signature, and the `--detail` gate.

resolution index so streamed parse batches resolve calls to imported symbols
defined in later batches.

cannot drift from what the in-batch path extracts. That costs one parse per

not for .ts, where it is most of a repository and an incremental map pays it for
every unchanged file too.

So the CLI now parses prescan sources on the worker pool it already runs for the
streaming loop and hands the results to buildGlobalResolutionIndex, which uses

**Note the conflict**: #382 landed while this was open and touched the same three places — `INDEX_PRESCAN_EXTENSIONS`, the parser-derived block in `buildGlobalResolutionIndex`, and `resolveEdges.test.ts`. I merged both rather than picking a side: the prescan set is now `.go .php .r .sas` + the six JS/TS extensions, and both cross-batch tests are kept.

## The perf fix

Your design decision — derive the index from real parse results rather than a regex, so it cannot drift from what the in-batch path extracts — is right, and I did not want to trade it away. The problem was only *where* the parsing happened: a synchronous main-thread loop inside `buildGlobalResolutionIndex`.

`buildGlobalResolutionIndex` now takes an optional `preParsed` map, and the CLI parses prescan sources on **the worker pool it is already running** for the streaming loop, handing the results in. Absent an entry, each language block falls back to parsing in-index, so tests and library callers behave exactly as before.

Measured on this repo, 180 JS/TS files:

```
index WITHOUT preParsed (main-thread parse): 1.24 s
index WITH preParsed (pool did the work):    0.001 s
```

The parse work still happens — it moved to the pool and spreads across cores instead of blocking. Applied to PHP, R and SAS too, since all four blocks had the same shape.

Added a test that supplies a parse result whose entity does not appear in the source text: it can only resolve if `preParsed` is genuinely used rather than re-parsed.

## Verification

- `core-ingestion`: **35 passed** in `resolveEdges.test.ts`; full suite 280 passed with the same 6 pre-existing failures you documented, no new ones
- `ix-cli`: **698 passed** across 52 files, `npm run typecheck` clean, lint 0 errors / 38 pre-existing warnings

## Still open, and worth its own issue rather than this PR

An incremental map still parses every prescanned file, not just the changed ones — it is parallel now instead of serial, but a one-file edit in a 5,000-file TypeScript repo still does 5,000 parses. The real fix is caching the per-file index keyed on mtime so unchanged files are never re-parsed, which needs cache invalidation and is a bigger change than belongs here. I'd rather land this and file that separately than hold a correct fix behind an optimisation.

I amended your commit rather than stacking, since the fix is threaded through the same lines; you are still the author and I added myself as co-author. Shout if you would rather it were split.

Thanks for contributing! The diagnosis here is correct and the index construction is careful — my one concern is the cost, which I think is larger than the 515-file validation repo could show.

## The part that's right

The JS/TS block mirrors the in-batch construction in `resolveEdges` exactly — same `kind === 'file' || kind === 'module'` filter, same `qualifiedKey(e)`, same name-keyed list of qkeys. That is the thing that usually drifts in this file (it is why the R and SAS blocks carry those "mirrors the qkMap construction at resolveEdges" comments), and you got it right, so cross-batch and in-batch resolution will agree on `dstQualifiedKey`. No correctness objection.

## The concern: this is the first prescan language where the prescan is the dominant cost

`buildGlobalResolutionIndex` calls `parseFile`, which is **synchronous tree-sitter on the main thread**. The streaming parse loop below it uses `ensureParsePool()` — a worker pool. So every JS/TS file now gets parsed twice: once serially in the prescan, once in parallel in the pool.

That trade was fine for the existing prescan set. Go uses a regex scan specifically to stay cheap, and R/SAS are niche and usually a small slice of a repo. JS/TS is the common case, and for a TypeScript repo it is ~all of the files.

Measured on this repo's own TS (176 files, 1.5 MB, `parseFile` via `core-ingestion/dist`):

```
SYNC prescan parse of all JS/TS: 1.02 s for 176 files  (~5.8 ms/file)
```

Extrapolating: ~5.8 s per 1,000 JS/TS files, ~29 s at 5,000 — single-threaded, before the parse pool starts.

**The incremental path is where this really bites.** In Path A:

```js
const remainingIndexFiles = filePaths.filter(fp => needsIndexPrescan(fp) && !changedSet.has(fp));
```

`filePaths` is the whole repo, so every *mtime-clean, unchanged* JS/TS file is read from disk and then synchronously parsed. Before this change `.ts` was not in `INDEX_PRESCAN_EXTENSIONS`, so `sources` and `remainingIndexFiles` were both empty and the cost was ~zero. After it, a one-file edit in a 5,000-file TS repo pays the full read + full serial parse on every `ix map`. That is the fast path this cache exists to protect.

At 515 files this is ~3 s and reads as acceptable, which I suspect is why it did not surface in your validation.

## Options, roughly in order of preference

1. **Run the prescan through the existing worker pool.** `ensureParsePool()` already exists in `ingest.ts` and is already parallel. It would need `buildGlobalResolutionIndex` to accept pre-parsed entities (or an async variant) rather than calling `parseFile` itself, since the pool lives in the CLI and this function is in `core-ingestion` — a bit of plumbing, but it removes both the double-parse and the serialization.
2. **Reuse the streaming loop's parse output.** The pool parses these files moments later anyway; only the ordering (index-before-batch) forces the duplicate.
3. **Narrow what gets prescanned.** Only files that are actually import targets of something in the changed set need to be in the index, which on an incremental map is a small fraction of the repo.
4. **Regex scan like Go.** Cheapest, but you deliberately avoided it for the drift reason above, and I think you were right to.

I do not think the fix has to be in this PR — but I would not want to land the JS/TS prescan without a plan for the incremental case, since that is the most common thing users do.

Happy to look again once you have picked a direction.

fix(ingest): do not let map mode delete the chunks it cannot rewrite

Three fixes on top of the deletion reconciliation.

1. `ix map` was destroying chunk data. stripMapModeOps drops every chunk
   UpsertNode from the patch but leaves DeleteNode alone, and chunk ids hash
   the chunk's start line — so any edit that shifts lines makes every
   downstream chunk look removed. Running `ix map` after an `ix ingest`
   therefore deleted the file's chunks and never recreated them: the cheap
   command silently destroying what the expensive one built. Chunks are not
   map mode's to reconcile, so reconcileRemovedEntities now takes a mapMode
   flag and leaves chunk nodes and CONTAINS_CHUNK/NEXT edges alone. The kind

   costs nothing extra.

2. Restored the empty-baseline guard, scoped. An empty mtime map is normally
   a discovery failure — an over-broad ignore rule, the wrong cwd — and
   persisting it discards the baseline and forces a full re-ingest. Dropping
   the guard outright to support "deleted the last file" made every such
   failure destructive. It now asks why the map is empty: with deletions
   recorded, empty is real; without them, discovery is assumed to have gone
   wrong.

3. Scoped the fail-closed hash lookup. Deleting from an unreliable baseline
   is how data gets lost, so failing closed there is right — but letting the
   throw escape aborted the whole map over one transient blip, taking the
   ordinary ingest of every changed file with it. The deletions are now
   dropped for that run and retried next time; the rest proceeds.

## 1. The blocker — map mode was destroying chunk data

`stripMapModeOps` drops every chunk `UpsertNode` but leaves `DeleteNode` alone, and `chunkId` hashes the chunk's start line. So any edit that shifts lines made every downstream chunk look removed, and `ix map` after an `ix ingest` deleted the file's chunks without recreating them — the cheap command silently destroying what the expensive one built.

`reconcileRemovedEntities` now takes a `mapMode` flag and leaves chunk nodes and `CONTAINS_CHUNK`/`NEXT` edges alone. ## 2. Empty-baseline guard — restored, but scoped

You dropped `mtimes.size === 0` so that deleting the last mapped file could persist an empty baseline. That case is real, but the guard was load-bearing for a different one: there is no `filePaths.length === 0` check anywhere in `ingestFiles`, so *any* discovery failure — over-broad ignore rule, wrong cwd — now overwrote a good baseline with an empty one.

It now asks **why** the map is empty: with deletions recorded this run, empty is a real state and is persisted; without them, discovery is assumed to have gone wrong and the baseline is kept. Your "persists an empty baseline after the last mapped file is deleted" test still passes unchanged, and I added its mirror image.

## 3. Fail-closed lookup — kept, narrowed

Failing closed before deleting is right; deleting from an unreliable baseline is how data gets lost. But letting the throw escape aborted the entire map over one transient blip, taking the ordinary ingest of every changed file with it. The deletions are now dropped for that run — they stay in the baseline and retry next time — and the rest proceeds.

- **Per-file round trips.** `sourcePatchIdCandidates` returns 25 ids tried serially, plus one `client.entity()` per removed node. Real, but batching it is a separate change and I did not want to bury the correctness fixes underneath it.
- **Op ordering.** `DeleteNode` still precedes the trailing `DeleteEdge`s for incident edges. I could not answer from the CLI side whether the backend cascades incident-edge removal on node delete — if it does, those trailing deletes target rows that are already gone. Worth confirming before anyone calls the ordering intentional.
- **Baseline write amplification.** `onCommitted` rewrites the whole baseline per deleted file. Bounded, and per-file durability is a defensible trade.

Stale-entity cleanup is a real gap and the overall shape here (compare the previous patch manifest, emit explicit deletions, track dependents so a recreated file heals its callers) is the right one. The tombstone `patchId` derivation is nicely done: deterministic per `(previousHash, deletionToken)` so a retry is idempotent but a later deletion is not, which is exactly the property you want.

## Blocker — `ix map` after `ix ingest` deletes chunk nodes and never recreates them

`reconcileRemovedEntities` runs **before** `stripMapModeOps`, at both call sites:

```js
patch = await reconcileRemovedEntities(client, patch, sourcePatchIdCandidates(...));
if (mapMode) patch = stripMapModeOps(patch);
```

`stripMapModeOps` filters out chunk `UpsertNode` ops but leaves `DeleteNode` ops untouched. And `chunkId` hashes the start line:

```js
chunkId: (filePath, chunkKind, name, startLine) =>
  deterministicId(`${ns}${normalizePath(filePath)}:chunk:${chunkKind}:${name ?? 'file_body'}:${startLine}`)
```

So any edit that shifts lines changes the chunk ids. Sequence: user runs `ix ingest` (chunks created), edits a file, runs `ix map`. Reconcile sees the old chunk ids missing from the new patch and emits deletions; the strip then removes the replacement upserts.

I confirmed this on your branch with the real `reconcileRemovedEntities` and a copy of `stripMapModeOps` — previous patch `[file-node, chunk-L1, chunk-L10]`, new patch upserting `[file-node, chunk-L1, chunk-L12]`:

```
DELETED : [ 'chunk-L10' ]
UPSERTED: [ 'file-node' ]
=> chunk nodes deleted but NOT recreated: [ 'chunk-L10' ]
```

Now the cheaper command silently destroys embedding/search data for every file it touches, and only a full `ix ingest` puts it back. Easiest fix is to skip reconciliation entirely in `mapMode`, or to filter chunk-node ids out of `removedNodeIds` when `mapMode` is set — `ix map` never owned that data and shouldn't be deleting it.

## Please reconsider — dropping the `mtimes.size === 0` guard

```js
- if (!ingestCompletedCleanly(parseErrors, commitErrors) || mtimes.size === 0) return false;
+ if (!ingestCompletedCleanly(parseErrors, commitErrors)) return false;
```

I understand why: an emptied repo has to be able to persist an empty baseline. But there is no `filePaths.length === 0` guard anywhere in `ingestFiles`, so *any* run that discovers zero files — an over-broad ignore rule, a bad `cwd`, a discovery glitch — now overwrites a good baseline with an empty one and forces a full re-ingest next time.

The `!fs.existsSync(filePath)` check on `deletedPaths` is a good safeguard and does stop this from turning into mass deletion, which I was glad to see. But the baseline still gets wiped. Gating on `mtimes.size > 0 || deletedPaths.length > 0` would keep the guard while still covering the case you actually need.

## Please reconsider — hash-lookup failure now aborts the whole map

```js
knownHashes = await loadExistingHashes(..., deletedPaths.length > 0);
```

With any deleted file present, a transient `getSourceHashes` failure throws instead of degrading to an empty map, so one network blip fails the entire ingest rather than just the deletion work. Failing closed on *deletion* is right — deleting from an unreliable baseline is how you lose data. But the scope is wider than the risk. Consider catching it and skipping deletion reconciliation for this run (leaving `deletedFiles` in the baseline so the next run retries) while letting the ordinary ingest proceed.

## Perf — per-file round-trips inside the patch loop

`reconcileRemovedEntities` now runs for every file with a `previousHash`, and it is serial I/O in what used to be a pure-CPU loop:

- `sourcePatchIdCandidates` returns **25** ids (current + 23 `PREVIOUS_EXTRACTORS` + legacy), tried one at a time until one is not a 404. Common case is 1 call, but the first `ix map` after a CLI upgrade walks the list for *every* changed file.
- then one `client.entity(nodeId)` per removed node, also serial.

A refactor that removes 50 symbols across 20 files pays 50 sequential `entity()` calls on top of the `getPatch` walk. Worth batching, or at least running the candidate probe concurrently.

## Smaller things

- **Op ordering.** `DeleteNode` ops are emitted before the `UpsertEdge` ops, and the `DeleteEdge` ops for incident edges come *after* the `DeleteNode`s. If the backend cascades incident-edge removal on node delete, those trailing `DeleteEdge`s target rows that are already gone — is that a no-op server-side, or an error? Worth confirming, since it decides whether the ordering is load-bearing.
- **Baseline write amplification.** `onCommitted` calls `saveIngestBaseline` once per committed deletion, rewriting the whole JSON each time. Deleting a directory of 500 files means 500 full rewrites. Durability per-file is a reasonable goal, but a debounce or a single write after the batch would be cheaper.
- **`readStoredPatchEntities` `data.ops` branch** treats `DeleteNode` ids from a previous patch as live entities. Harmless (they re-delete), but it means a tombstone-follows-tombstone sequence re-emits deletions for already-removed nodes.

The branch is currently conflicting with `main` and will need a rebase.

The test coverage is genuinely good — `planDeletedFileRecovery`, the retry-idempotency assertion on the tombstone id, and the "fails closed when the previous patch has no entity manifest" case are all the right things to pin. Once the map-mode chunk issue is sorted I would be happy to take another pass.

## 1. Nullable types silently fall back to bare names

The queries match `type: (named_type (name) @_typed_var_type)`, but `?Service` does not parse as `named_type` — it is `optional_type` wrapping it:

```
private ?Service $s;   → (property_declaration type: (optional_type (named_type (name))) ...)
private Service $s;    → (property_declaration type: (named_type (name)) ...)
```

So on your branch:

```php

  private ?Service $s;
  public function go(): void { $this->s->create(); }
}
```
resolves to `C.go -> create` rather than `C.go -> Service.create`. Given `?Type` is idiomatic for any nullable dependency, I would expect this to be a large share of real member calls.

The typed-parameter pattern is rooted at `(method_declaration ...)`, so a top-level `function` gets nothing:


```
(property_declaration
  type: [(named_type (name) @_typed_var_type)
         (optional_type (named_type (name) @_typed_var_type))]
  (property_element
    name: (variable_name (name) @_typed_var_name))) @_typed_var_scope

  type: [(named_type (name) @_typed_var_type)
         (optional_type (named_type (name) @_typed_var_type))]
  name: (variable_name (name) @_typed_var_name)) @_typed_var_scope

; Typed parameters on methods and plain functions: function run(?Service $s)
[(method_declaration
   parameters: (formal_parameters
     [(simple_parameter
       type: [(named_type (name) @_typed_param_type)
              (optional_type (named_type (name) @_typed_param_type))]
       name: (variable_name (name) @_typed_param_name))

       type: [(named_type (name) @_typed_param_type)
              (optional_type (named_type (name) @_typed_param_type))]
       name: (variable_name (name) @_typed_param_name))]))

   parameters: (formal_parameters
     (simple_parameter
       type: [(named_type (name) @_typed_param_type)

       name: (variable_name (name) @_typed_param_name))))] @_typed_param_scope
```

## Summary

Recovery for **#385**, reported by @RMA1313. `ix upgrade` on any version before 0.9.0 refreshed only the *bash* shim under Git Bash and left `%IX_HOME%\bin\ix.cmd` aimed at a `cli\ix.cmd` that the same upgrade had replaced with a version-nested directory. All cmd.exe offers is:

```text
'"C:\Users\Win 10\.ix\bin\..\cli\ix.cmd"' is not recognized as an internal or external command, operable program or batch file.
```

which names the wrapper rather than the cause, and reads like a broken install rather than a broken upgrade.

**This one cannot be fixed forward.** `ix upgrade` is executed by the version being upgraded *from*, so nothing shipped today reaches the installs that break — and once broken, `ix doctor` is exactly as unreachable as `ix`. The only thing the user can still run is the batch file, so the recovery instruction has to live there.

Root cause is the layout bug fixed in #346 (v0.9.0); this PR is about the population that upgrades *into* the fix from below it.

## Type
- [x] Bug fix

## Changes
- `windowsShimBody()` — the launcher checks its target before invoking it and, when it is gone, prints what happened plus `irm https://ix-infra.com/install.ps1 | iex`.
- **It also propagates `%errorlevel%`**, which the old one-line body silently swallowed. Every non-zero `ix` exit — a failed map, a Pro stub — had been reported to callers as success. Unrelated to #385, found while writing it.
- `install.ps1` and `refreshLaunchers()` both emit that body, with a test asserting they stay byte-identical. They have drifted before: the flat-vs-nested shim bugs (#346, #385) were each one writer knowing something the other did not.

Three of the eight open code scanning alerts — the ones with a real fix behind them. The other five are dispositions rather than code changes; they are listed at the bottom so the whole set is accounted for in one place.

## #44 — `js/file-system-race` (high), `view.ts`

`readRunningPort` called `existsSync(PORT_FILE)` and then, fifteen lines later, wrote to that same path. That pair is what CodeQL flagged, and the check could always go stale before the operation — it never told us the read would succeed either.

The reads now go straight out through `readTextIfPresent`, which returns null **only** for ENOENT and rethrows everything else. That distinction is load-bearing: both callers of `readAlivePid` treat null as licence to act, so collapsing "unreadable" into "absent" means `ix view stop` deletes a live server's state and `ix view` spawns a second one it cannot record. `readRunningPort` keeps its swallow-all policy deliberately — it is looking up a URL to print, not liveness — and now says so. The scope read also stops reading a zero-length file as a workspace named `""`.

## #47 — `js/http-to-file-access` (medium), `ingest-baseline.ts`

The rev arrives off the backend's commit response and only the read side ever checked its shape, so a non-integer rev (an older backend answering `"9"` instead of `9`) cleared a bare `> 0` and was written, then rejected on the next read.

The save side is the *last* stop, though, not the first. The same value enters at the accumulator, where a bare `>` compares it as a string — `"9"` becomes the max, and `"10" > "9"` is then false, so the max walks backwards — and it ships to the user verbatim as the `latestRev` field of `ix ingest --format json`. `advanceRev` screens it where it enters, which fixes the max, the JSON contract and the persisted baseline in one place. `isRev` is now a single predicate both sides of the baseline share; they previously sat three lines apart and disagreed on whether 0 was valid.

To be accurate about the cost: `currentRev` is read only by `ix status`'s Revision line. Incremental skipping runs off the mtime map, which was always persisted correctly. A bad rev means a wrong Revision, **not** a re-ingest.

`nanoid` 3.3.16 → 3.3.18 and `brace-expansion` 5.0.7 → 5.0.9, clearing all three advisories behind the alert: GHSA-2v37-7h3g-55p8, GHSA-mh99-v99m-4gvg, GHSA-rgw5-rvv9-x895. Lockfiles only; both are dev-only transitive deps, and `npm audit` is clean in `ix-cli` and `core-ingestion`.

entities.human_summary: fix(cli): register the patches command instead of stubbing it — RESOLVED.
entities.deep_summary:
## The bug

`ix-cli` has always contained a complete `ix patches` — client call, `--limit`, `--format text|json|llm`, and `formatPatches` already has a working `llm` branch (`format.ts:242`).

It was never imported by `register/oss.ts`. Meanwhile `patches` sat in `PRO_COMMANDS`, so `registerProStubs` installed the "requires Ix Pro" sentinel over the top of it.

So OSS users got a paywall message for a command this repo ships. Nobody noticed because the stub is a *plausible* answer — had it fallen through to commander's `unknown command` the way `goals` did (#384), it would have been reported long ago.

Found by @Alot1z while writing the agent skill (#368).

## The fix

Register it, and drop it from `PRO_COMMANDS`.

## The part worth reviewing

`@ix/pro` registers a `patches` too. Commander **throws** on a duplicate command name, and Pro's `tryRegister` wraps registration in a `try`/`catch` that swallows it — so on a Kartr install the OSS registration (which runs first, from `registerOssCommands`) is the one that survives, and Pro's is silently skipped.

That is the outcome we want: this version also supports `--format llm`, which Pro's does not. But it means the two implementations' behaviour now matters, so this one uses the same `createClient()` factory Pro's does instead of constructing `IxClient` directly. They are identical today (`createClient` is literally `new IxClient(getEndpoint())`) — the point is that its docstring says Pro commands should prefer it "so auth and endpoint resolution can evolve in one spot", and `patches` is now a command both editions route through.

Verified the swallow rather than assuming it: commander 12.1.0 raises `cannot add command 'patches' as already have command 'patches'` from `_registerCommand`, and `tryRegister`'s `catch` covers the `fn(program)` call, not just the `import`.

## Tests

The stub test asserting `patches` reports Pro is replaced by one asserting it is **not** stubbed. A stub for a command that exists in OSS shadows the real implementation, and because `registerOssCommands` runs first the symptom is silence, not a crash — worth pinning so it cannot come back.

722 tests green. `ix patches --help` verified against a real build.

## Docs

CLAUDE.md said the wrong thing in three places: the gotcha claiming `ix patches` is an unknown command, the `[Pro]` marker on its routing row, and the "only the first three work without Pro" line above that table.

Fixes #371

entities.human_summary: fix(upgrade): stop comparing compass versions across two unrelated series — RESOLVED.
entities.deep_summary:
## The bug

`compass/.version` is written by two producers in two different version series, and recorded no way to tell them apart:

| producer | writes | series |
|---|---|---|
| `release.yml` | the **Ix** version (`0.9.2`) | Ix |
| `install.sh` / `install.ps1` / the compass-upgrade path | the **ix-compass-dist** release (`0.3.0`) | compass |

`isNewer(compassLatest, compassCurrent)` compared whichever happened to be on disk against the dist series. That is correct only while Ix's numbers are the larger ones. **The first ix-compass-dist tag above the running Ix version** — a v1.0.0, or just a v0.9.2 — makes `isNewer` true and replaces a *newer* bundled compass with an older dist build.

Same class as #365/#366, reached from the other end: there the stamp was missing so `current` read as `none`; here the stamp is present but denominated in the wrong series.

## It is not only latent

`install.sh` stamped every install with the latest **dist** release number regardless of where the compass came from. The compass it installs always comes from the release tarball — so it mislabelled a release bundle as a dist build, and clobbered the correct stamp the tarball already carried.

Reproduced on a live v0.9.x install:

```
~/.ix/cli/compass/.version   → 0.2.0     # written by install.sh, from ix-compass-dist
~/.ix/.version-check.json    → compassLatest: 0.3.0
```

`ix` prints "Compass update available" and `ix upgrade` would replace a bundle built from system-compass `main` at v0.9.x release time with dist v0.3.0.

## The fix

The stamp declares its own provenance, and the comparison only runs where it means something:

```
source=release        source=dist
ix=0.9.3              version=0.3.0
compass=7f98724
```

**A release bundle is never replaced by a dist download.** It was built from `main` when the CLI was cut, so it is at least as new as any dist release published before it; one published after arrives with the next Ix release, which bundles `main` again.

The dist download stays the **repair** path for a missing or gutted bundle. That still fires: `getInstalledCompassVersion()` reports `0.0.0` when `index.html` is absent, which no real release number matches.

## Backwards compatibility

A bare number is a legacy stamp — everything shipped up to and including v0.9.2 — and reads as **dist-series**. That is what `install.sh` wrote, it is the majority of installs in the wild, and it leaves them exactly as correct as they are today. Release-bundled legacy stamps stay accidentally-correct until compass-dist passes the Ix version, i.e. no worse than before. New releases carry the explicit form and are immune.

## Why the commit, not a version

`system-compass`'s `package.json` version is not maintained against the dist release series — it reads `0.2.0` while dist is on `v0.3.0` (built from `7f98724`). So stamping the package version would have been a third wrong number. The commit is the only reliable identity the bundle has, and it is passed from the `compass` job to `build` as a job output.

## Both installers stop calling ix-compass-dist

Neither ever installs from there, so neither needs to know what it has published. `resolve_compass_version` / `Get-CompassLatestVersion` are removed. `ix upgrade` asks that question, at the one point where it can also tell which series the installed bundle belongs to.

Each installer now prefers the stamp the tarball shipped with, and only writes one if the bundle has none.

## Tests

`upgrade-compass-stamp.test.ts` — release form, dist form, bare legacy number, empty/malformed, CRLF (how a Windows bundle arrives), and a case pinning the inversion itself.

728 tests green. `bash -n` and `sh -n` clean on install.sh; release.yml parses and `needs.compass.outputs.sha` resolves in the `build` job.

Fixes #376

I ran the new format through `origin/main`'s own `isNewer`:

```
dist 0.3.0 vs release-stamp 0.9.4 -> isNewer=false
dist 0.3.0 vs release-stamp 1.0.0 -> isNewer=TRUE
dist 0.3.0 vs release-stamp 1.1.0 -> isNewer=TRUE
dist 0.3.0 vs legacy bare  0.9.4 -> isNewer=false
```

`splitVersion` yields `Number("source=release\nix=1") = NaN -> 0` for the major, so a 1.x release parses as `[0,0,0]`. entities.deep_summary:
## Why

#349 is a Windows install that died after extraction because TEMP arrived in 8.3 short form (`C:\Users\WIN10\~1\...`) on a profile named `C:\Users\Win 10`. The reporter confirmed that pointing `TEMP`/`TMP` at a path without a space let the same install finish.

#352 moved `install.ps1`'s scratch off TEMP for that reason — and said so in its own comment:

> Note `ix upgrade` still stages through `os.tmpdir()` (upgrade.ts), which on Windows is TEMP verbatim. If this class is real, it is unfixed there.

This is that half. It is the worse of the two places for the failure to bite: a failed install leaves a machine with no Ix on it, but a **failed upgrade breaks an install that was working** — which is exactly the shape of #385.

## What changed

Both download directories move to `IX_HOME`, joining the staging and backup directories already there. `IX_HOME` comes from `USERPROFILE` in its long form. `mkdirSync(IX_HOME)` first, because a first upgrade after a manual install can reach this before anything has created it.

`sweepUpgradeOrphans` learns `.cli-download-` and `.compass-download-`. Leaving TEMP also leaves the OS's own cleanup, so without this an upgrade killed mid-download parks a multi-MB archive in `~/.ix` forever.

The prefixes are deliberately `-download-` and not `-backup-`: `recover()` renames the newest `.cli-backup-*` over the install directory, and an archive must never be a candidate for that. There is already a test pinning that reasoning for `install.ps1`'s zip; this adds the matching one.

## The part I nearly broke

**The sweep call had to move above the download.** It sat between the download and the extract, which was safe only while the scratch lived in `os.tmpdir()`. Once the sweep reclaims `.cli-download-*`, from that position it deletes the archive it is about to extract — breaking *every* upgrade on every platform, not just Windows.

Caught while tracing the ordering rather than by a test, so there is now a test for it. Above the download, the sweep also puts an interrupted install back even when the download then fails, which the old order could not do. ## Blocking: a failed download can delete the user's only working compass

`cleanupCompassSwap:615` tests `existsSync(join(compassDir, "index.html"))` and its comment is explicit about why: a `compass/` holding only a `.version` is a real state, and a bare `existsSync` "would call that 'back in place' and drop a backup the caller had just told the user to go and rescue."

`recover()` inside `sweepUpgradeOrphans` uses exactly that bare `existsSync(dest)`. So with `compass/` left as a `.version`-only husk and `.compass-backup-1234` holding the only real bundle, `recover()` declines to restore, and the loop below then deletes the backup.

On `main` that sweep ran *after* a successful download, so an offline run exited before reaching it and the backup survived for the next attempt. Hoisting the sweep above `curl` means **a run that installs nothing now destroys it** — the user sees only "[error] Failed to download", and `ix view` is permanently blank with no copy left on disk.

The two tests can't see this because they never construct the husk. Aligning `recover`'s test with `cleanupCompassSwap`'s (`index.html`, not bare `existsSync`) fixes it and makes the two agree.

## Blocking: concurrent `ix upgrade` deletes an in-flight download

The scratch moved from `os.tmpdir()`, where no sweep could match it, into `IX_HOME` with a swept prefix. Process A creates `.cli-download-AAAAAA` and starts a curl with a 300s timeout; process B — a second terminal, or `bootstrap.sh` re-running `ix upgrade` when it finds compass missing — calls `prepareDownloadDir` and deletes A's directory wholesale. On Linux/macOS curl's fd stays valid so A exits 0, then `tar -xzf` hits a missing path and A reports "Failed to extract CLI update" on a good download.

`.cli-staging-<pid>` has the same shape on main, but its window is the few seconds of extraction; this one is the whole download. Some ownership marker (pid in the name, skipped when that pid is live) would close both.

- `prepareDownloadDir` in the compass branch is the first filesystem write under `IX_HOME` and sits *outside* the try/catch that deliberately keeps compass failures non-fatal. #349's reporter is on `C:\Users\Win 10` and their confirmed workaround was pointing TEMP at a space-free path.
